newsitem.title: USA: Playboy seeks Telecommunications Act ruling.
newsitem.headline: Playboy seeks Telecommunications Act ruling.

text.p: Playboy Entertainment Group said Wednesday it would file a motion for summary judgment to declare a section of the Telecommunications Act of 1996 on adult-theme broadcasting unconstitutional.
The company said it was taking the step in light of the U.S. Supreme Court's decision invalidating regulation of "indecent" and "patently offensive" speech on the Internet.

"We believe that Section 505 (of the Telecommunications Act) is unconstitutional for the same reasons that the Supreme Court found the Communications Decency Act to be invalid. Section 505 was adopted at the same time as the CDA, and it incorporated exactly the same defective legal standard," Christie Hefner, chairman and chief executive of Playboy Enterprises Inc, said in a statement.
Playboy had filed a friend of the court brief with the Supreme Court on the Internet case, arguing there was an inherent vagueness to the indecency standard.

Shortly after the the Telecommunications Act was passed into law last year, Playboy obtained a temporary restraining order preventing enforcement of Section 505. In November, the U.S. District Court in Wilmington, Del., denied Playboy's request for a preliminary injunction, so the company appealed the ruling to the Supreme Court. The District Court subsequently issued an order blocking enforcement of Section 505 pending Supreme Court review. That stay was lifted by the U.S. Federal Communications Commission in May, after the Supreme Court declined to review the earlier ruling.

Since then, Playboy has returned to the Wilmington court to seek a permanent injunction. The Supreme Court's Internet ruling is the basis for Playboy's latest motion, a motion for summary judgment, which was filed today.
